# Question

**Does turning up the music in a bar cause people to drink more beer?** Guéguen et al. (2008, *Alcoholism: Clin Exp Res*) observed 40 male beer patrons in a bar on nights with the sound level at 88 vs 72 dB, recording glasses consumed and time per glass.

## Data source

Group means reproduced exactly from the paper; the 20/20 per-patron split and SDs are a documented reconstruction. Naturalistic field experiment — sound level varied by night, not randomized per patron.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Glasses of beer consumed per patron by sound level"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="condition", y="glasses", hue="condition",
            palette=["#8fbf8f", "#c76c6c"], legend=False, ax=ax)
sns.stripplot(data=df, x="condition", y="glasses", color="0.25", size=4, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Sound level")
ax.set_ylabel("Glasses consumed")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Welch two-mean tests on both outcomes, normal approximation and 100k-replicate randomization, bootstrap CIs of the differences.

| Outcome | 88 dB vs 72 dB | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Glasses consumed | +0.80 glasses | Welch t(37.8) = 2.97, **p = 0.005**; randomization p = 0.009 |
| Time per glass | −3.06 min | Welch t ≈ −4.9, **p < 1e-4**; randomization p < 1e-4 |

# Decision

**Louder music → faster drinking**: patrons drank more glasses because each glass took less time. Effect small but reliable; the causal reading is suggestive since patrons were not individually randomized to sound levels.
